title: Normal-Tension Glaucoma (NTG): The Clinical Masterclass
summary: A comprehensive guide to Normal-Tension Glaucoma, a subtype of Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma where progressive optic neuropathy occurs despite statistically normal intraocular pressure. Often considered a disease of ocular perfusion and structural susceptibility.

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: NTG is defined as progressive glaucomatous optic neuropathy with characteristic visual field defects and disc changes, occurring in patients with an intraocular pressure (IOP) consistently measured at or below 21 mmHg on diurnal testing. It is a diagnosis of exclusion.

sections.title: Red Flags: Non-Glaucomatous Causes
content: Unilateral visual field loss (strongly suggests space-occupying lesion)
Pallor of the neuroretinal rim out of proportion to cupping
Visual acuity loss (typically spared in early NTG)
Color vision defects disproportionate to field loss
Presence of vertical visual field defects (neurological until proven otherwise)

sections.title: Clinical Examination & Findings
content: Splinter (Drance) hemorrhages on the optic nerve head
Peripapillary atrophy (Beta-zone/Alpha-zone)
Deeper, more focal neuroretinal rim notches
Higher prevalence of disc drusen
Greater susceptibility to progressive loss at low pressures

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: Step 1: Multiple diurnal IOP measurements (to rule out spikes).
Step 2: Pachymetry (Correct for CCT).
Step 3: Gonioscopy (Verify open angle).
Step 4: Humphrey Visual Field (HVF 24-2).
Step 5: OCT Disc/RNFL Analysis.
Step 6: MRI/CT (If suspicious for neurological etiology).

sections.title: Treatment Protocol (Collaborative Normal Tension Glaucoma Study)
content: Goal: Lower baseline IOP by at least 30%.
Step 1: Topical Monotherapy (Prostaglandin Analogs - Latanoprost/Bimatoprost).
Step 2: Add Second Agent (Beta-blockers or Alpha-agonists).
Step 3: Consider Laser Trabeculoplasty (ALT/SLT) for adjunctive support.
Step 4: Surgical intervention (Trabeculectomy/MIGS) if progression persists.

content.explanation: V: Vasospastic (Raynaud's), A: Apnea (Sleep), S: Systemic Hypotension, C: Cardiovascular diseases/Coagulation issues.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: NTG disc changes often appear more 'focal' compared to 'diffuse' damage in High-Tension Glaucoma.
Always evaluate for nocturnal systemic hypotension in patients with rapid progression.
Patients with NTG have a significantly higher prevalence of migraine and cold-induced peripheral vasospasm.
Treatment is indicated even if IOP is 'normal' if the optic nerve shows signs of structural or functional progression.
